why: Each chapter needs ceil(pages[i]/p) days of coverage, and a day adds one coverage to a length-k window. Sweeping left to right, the left-most chapter still short of coverage must be covered by windows that start at it (clamped to n-k), so place them there greedily and track active windows with a difference array. The week's sliding-window idea shows up as the range-add, not as binary search.
hints: Turn pages into a count: chapter i must be inside a chosen window ceil(pages[i] / p) times. Order of days does not matter.

Scan from the left. If chapter i is still short by x covers, every window that can still help and also helps the most future chapters starts at i (or at n-k if i is past the last start). Add x such windows.
Keep a difference array: when adding x windows starting at s, add x to the running coverage now and subtract x at s+k. Sum all x. O(n) time, answer can exceed 32-bit.
pitfalls: Windows cannot start after n-k; chapters near the right end must be covered by the window that starts at n-k.
Use ceiling division; reading less than p pages in a day still costs a full day.
The answer can reach about 10^5 * 10^9, so it needs a 64-bit integer in other languages.
